division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.46(1)  On service of a third party claim,
(a) the third party defendant becomes a party to the action
between the plaintiff and the defendant, and
(b) all subsequent proceedings in the action must name the
third party as a party in the action between the plaintiff
and the defendant.
(2)  The pleadings between
(a) the defendant and the third party defendant, and
(b) a third party plaintiff and a third party defendant,
form part of the court file between the plaintiff and the defendant.
(3)  A third party claim must be tried with the other claims in the
action unless the Court otherwise orders under rule 3.71.

BOOK_A.title: Third Party Defendant Becomes Party
BOOK_A.defined_terms: claim, Court, defendant, party, plaintiff, third party defendant, third party plaintiff
BOOK_A.commentary:
Rule 3.46 gives a third party full status as a party to the main suit. On the implications of that for costs, see theNicklescase. Counsel for third parties do not always take full advantage of that

status;sometimes they merely defend the third party proceeding and do not try to defend the main suit as allowed by R.3.49(1)(c). Usually a plaintiff who fails does not pay costs of third party proceedings, unless joinder of the third party was required and inevitable. The right level of Schedule C (i.e.which column) is set by

the amount which the statement of claim claims, and that may apply also to costs payable to a third party.A third party notice exposes the third parties to liability for the sum claimed, and the test for their costs is whether the third-party notice followed naturally and inevitably from the main action, i.e.whether the defendant had no real alternative but to join the third parties.The plaintiff sued the developer, who had all work done by contractors so it was inevitable they would be third-partied.

A successful plaintiff may get costs from the defendant occasioned by the defendant's third party notice. If the third party only comes into the suit because of the defendant's counterclaim, which fails, the defendant may have to pay any costs which the plaintiff incurs in relation to the third party.

Third party proceedings can become complex, especially if there are fourth and fifth parties. Who goes first at trial, and how to avoid duplication, become contentious.The court's directions are useful, even necessary, especially if the third and fourth party proceedings are slowing a simple main action, or if there is some reason that the entire thing should not be dealt with in a single trial.

1Double N Earthmovers v.Edmonton (City)2005 ABCA 104, 363 AR 201. 2Chiarella v. Klymok2011 ABQB 814. The plaintiff cannot get judgment directly against the third party.

TheInsurance Actgives similar rights to an insurer added by order as a "third party".

*Third Party Defendant's Options*

commentary.text: Rule 3.46 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.46. 1. Pierringer Agreement In Canadian Natural Resources Limited v. Wood Group Mustang (Canada) Inc. (IMV Projects Inc.), 2018 ABCA 305, 2018 CarswellAlta 2079, Justice Slatter explained Pierringer agreements and compared them to Mary Carter agreements: 119 In the month immediately before the trial, CNRL entered into Pierringer settlement agreements with Shaw Pipe and Flint Field Services. Under a Pierringer agreement, the plaintiff enters into final settlements with some of the defendants, who withdraw from the litigation. The plaintiff then proceeds to trial against the non-settling defendants: Pierringer v Hoger, 124 NW 2d 106 (1963 SC Wisconsin). The settling defendants agree to pay a sum of money, they are no longer parties to the action, and the plaintiff agrees not to pursue the non-settling defendants for more than their proportionate liability. Since the non-settling defendants cannot be liable for more than their proportionate share of the damage, the settling defendants are not exposed to any claim for contribution from the non-settling defendants. 120 There are many variations of partial settlement agreements: CCS Corp. v Secure Energy Services Inc., 2016 ABQB 94 at para. 32, 83 CPC (7th) 126. Pierringer agreements can be contrasted with another common type, Mary Carter agreements: Booth v Mary Carter Paint Co., 202 So 2d 8 (1967 Fl Dist CA). In a Mary Carter agreement, the plaintiff is guaranteed a fixed recovery from the settling defendants, but the settling defendants remain parties to the action and seek to maximize recovery from the non-settling defendants. The settling defendants' exposure is capped at the agreed amount, but the settling defendants' obligation decreases in direct proportion to any increase in the non-settling defendants' liability as determined at trial. Justice Slatter then made this observation about Pierringer agreements (at paragraphs 125 and 127): [125]… the existing rule in Bedard v. Amin[2010 ABCA 3], which provides that the plaintiff must account to the non-settling defendants if it “over settled”. In other words, if a settling defendant agrees to pay the plaintiff more than the trial judge finds that settling defendant would have been liable for, the non-settling defendant is entitled to credit for that “overpayment” in order to avoid the plaintiff being double compensated. … … [127]… The effect of Bedard v. Amin is that the risk of a Pierringer settlement falls on the plaintiff. If the plaintiff “under-recovers” from the settling defendants, it will not be able to make up that shortfall from the non-settling defendants. On the other hand, if the plaintiff “over-recovers” from the settling defendants (as in Bedard v. Amin) it will not be allowed to keep the surplus. The Court declined to overrule Bedard v. Amin (see paragraph 148). In Slaferek v. TCG International Inc. (1997), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 279 (Q.B.), Clarke J. explained a Pierringer agreement. The plaintiffs commenced an action against the defendants who brought third parties into the action. The plaintiff ultimately settled with the third parties (referred to by Clarke J. as “the other third parties”). That settlement agreement contained terms which limited the liability of the other third parties in the both the main action and the contribution and indemnity proceedings (the settlement amount), and further obligated the plaintiff to indemnify the other third parties for any amount in excess of the settlement amount ultimately found owing to the plaintiff or the defendants by the other third parties. The other third parties successfully sought from Clarke J. an order striking out the third party notice. In the course of deciding to strike the third party notice, Clarke J. said, at pp. 285-86: Finally, the Other Third Parties describe the nature of their arrangement with the Plaintiff Darin Slaferek as a Pierringer agreement. In that regard, they were referring to the case of Pierringer v. Hoger (1963), 124 N.W. 2d 106 in the Supreme Court of Wisconsin. That case involved an action arising out of an explosion wherein the settling tort feasors moved for summary judgment to dismiss cross-complaints of non-settling tort feasors for contribution. At pp. 111-112 the Court had this to say: … The issue between the plaintiff and the non-settling defendant which should be framed by an amendment to the pleadings is the percentage of causal negligence, if any, of the non-settling defendant, but such percentage of negligence can only be determined by a proper allocation of all of the causal negligence, if any, of all the joint feasors and of the plaintiff if contributory negligence is involved. The determination of this issue between the plaintiff and the non-settling defendant does not require the settling defendants to remain parties because the allocation, if any, of the casual negligence of the settling tort feasors is merely a part of the mechanics by which the percentage of causal negligence of the non-settling tort feasors is determined. It makes no practical difference to the settling tort feasors what percentage of casual negligence is allocated to them because they have bought their peace in any event… Upon the trial the release should be given immediate effect as it is for contribution purposes and the judgment if any against the non-settling defendants should only be for that percentage of negligence allocated to him by the findings or the verdict. The claim for the balance has been satisfied by the plaintiff and there is no point going through this circuitry of ordering a judgment for a larger amount and requiring the plaintiff to satisfy it… The objectives of a Pierringer agreement for the Other Third Parties of course are to set a limit upon their liability and to reduce the cost in terms of both money and personnel involved in litigating the matter. The objective for the administration of justice is to focus the issues the Court will be required to deal with to a determination of what negligence if any can the Plaintiff Darin Slaferek bring home to Calido [the defendant] and if so what percentage of overall negligence should be borne by Calido. The end result should be a shorter and more efficient trial. All of these objectives in my view are ones that this Court should encourage. Mr. Justice Langston discussed Pierringer agreements, and Mary Carter agreements in Vandevelde v. Smith (1999), 243 A.R. 161 (Q.B.). At p. 164, His Lordship said: The position adopted by the court in Pierringer… is consistent with the view that such agreements limit the liability of the nonsettling defendants to a question of their own several liability. It would appear that the nonsettling defendants do not run the risk of joint liability with the settling parties, since this fact is effectively precluded by the nature of the agreement. Langston J. then specifically commented on Slaferek v. TCG International Inc. (1997), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 279 (Q.B.). At pp. 166-67, he said: In my view Slaferek does not stand for the principle that a nonsettling defendant is precluded from third party action as against a settling defendant because of the provisions of a Pierringer agreement. In Slaferek the plaintiff was proceeding only as against the nonsettling defendant, for its separate individual negligence. It is clear that since the plaintiff had satisfied its claim with the settlors there was no issue of contribution. In Slaferek the court commented on the affect of a Pierringer agreement and suggested that such agreements would focus the issues which the court will be required to deal with and those issues were the determination of what negligence if any can the plaintiff bring home to the remaining defendant, and if so, what percentage of the overall negligence should be born by the remaining defendant. Efforts by one of several tortfeasors to settle with a plaintiff have seen the evolution of two types of agreements, one is the Pierringer agreement the other is termed a “Mary Carter” Agreement which is based on the Florida case of Booth v. Mary Carter Paint Co. (1967), 202 So.2d 8 (Fla. App.). In a Mary Carter agreement the settlor guarantees that the plaintiff will recover a sum certain and it thereby limits its own exposure. The settlor's liability is reduced in proportion to any increase in the nonsettling defendants' liability. The settlor remains a party to the action and may even actively help the plaintiff in its efforts to maximize the damages against the nonsettlors. While the two types of agreements are similar in that they are settlement agreements between a plaintiff and one of several joint tortfeasors, they differ in that under a Pierringer agreement the settling defendant is no longer a party to the action and it is implicit in the agreement that the plaintiff will not pursue the nonsettling defendants for that portion, if any, of liability assessed by the trial judge against the settling party. The settlor gains the advantage of having his liability fixed and therefore not running the risk of paying one hundred (100%) per cent of any joint and several judgment. The issue which remains, and is central to this application is the impact which a Pierringer agreement may have on third party proceedings. The agreement is a contract made after the commencement of litigation to which the nonsettlors are not a party but which may affect their rights adversely. The nature of the agreement, and its timing, may effectively preclude discovery of the settlors and this would affect the nonsettlor's ability to establish negligence on the part of the settling parties. As with a Mary Carter agreement the settling party may be actively engaged in assisting the plaintiff in its efforts to maximize the percentage of liability attributed to the nonsettling party. A review of the decisions in Pierringer and Slaferek clearly suggest that the essence of a Pierringer agreement is the elimination of the settling parties' involvement in the litigation. The result in both cases was the elimination of third party participation in the proceedings. While it is clear that the defendants are not a party to the Pierringer agreements, it is equally clear that their rights may be directly affected by the obligations created in the Pierringer agreements. The means by which third parties were eliminated in both Pierringer and Slaferek illustrates this point. In each case the plaintiff restricted its action to the several liability of the nonsettling defendant. In each case there were provisions for indemnifying the settling parties. The consequence of the plaintiffs' actions was that the third parties were not exposed to any liability either from the plaintiff nor from third party actions. Applications to strike the third party proceedings would not affect the position of the remaining parties and would clarify the issue before the courts. Thus in a circuitous, but effective manner, the plaintiff can arbitrarily affect a nonsettling defendant's rights by completely shielding a third party's exposure. This is clearly in keeping with the intent of Pierringer agreements and this has been the result in cases where Pierringer agreements have been utilized. There is nothing sinister in this process since, at the end of the day, the nonsettling defendant need only address his several liability. However the one real handicap which a nonsettling defendant faces is the issue of the manner in which he is able to prove the degree of his several negligence as it relates to the several negligence of the settling party. Depending upon the timing of the Pierringer agreement the nonsettling defendant may be placed in the position that it is unable to discover a third party who is hastily withdrawn from the proceedings. This issue however, is not unlike situations frequently encountered in litigation where parties may be handicapped in their ability to fully bring forth information which they view as being favourable. The application to amend, as presently advanced by the plaintiff, purports to rely on the Pierringer agreements entered into between the plaintiff and the settling defendants. A review of those agreements does not disclose a requirement for such an application by the plaintiff. A review of the circumstances surrounding this application does not suggest that amending the pleadings as proposed by the plaintiff would in any way clarify the issues with which a trial court must deal. Striking the names of the settling defendants and striking references to their potential liability is not particularly efficacious since those parties remain as litigants by virtue of their third party status. In my view it is proper for the trial judge to have a full understanding of the complexities of the litigation, particularly in view of the fact that he may well have to deal with the apportionment of liability. The agreements, through those portions which do require the plaintiff to make amendments, may well affect the nonsettling defendant's ability to deal with the conduct of their defence. A partial amendment at this juncture, in my view, may well prejudice the defendants' position. The plaintiff is clearly entitled to discontinue as against parties named in a Statement of Claim. Such a discontinuance does not necessarily mandate that there need be an amendment to the pleadings. Courts frequently deal with such situations and the fact that individuals identified in pleadings are no longer parties to the action does not necessarily impact upon the proceedings. In Amoco Canada Petroleum Co. v. Propak Systems Ltd., 1999 ABQB 716, 1999 CarswellAlta 891, 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 194; affirmed 2001 ABCA 110, 2001 CarswellAlta 575, 281 A.R. 185, 91 Alta. L.R. (3d) 13; leave to appeal refused 2002 CarswellAlta 522, 2002 CarswellAlta 523, 312 A.R. 398 (note) (S.C.C.), at pp. 196-97 [Alta. L.R.], Hart J. gave the following explanation of a Pierringer agreement: The type of settlement agreement reached by the settling parties in this case apparently originated in the case of Pierringer v. Hoger, 124 N.W. 2d 106 (U.S. Wis. S.C. 1963), a decision of the Supreme Court of Wisconsin in October of 1963. In Hudson Bay Mining & Smelting Co. v. Fluor Daniel Wright (1997), 120 Man. R. (2d) 214 (Man. Q.B.), the Manitoba Court of Queen's Bench identified the essential features of a Pierringer Agreement at page 222 to be (a) segregation of the contracting defendant's liability; (b) satisfaction of the contracting defendant's liability to the credit of all parties to the litigation; (c) the plaintiff's ability to continue with the action against the remaining defendants; (d) the plaintiff's agreement that it will indemnify the contracting defendant for any contribution it pays to the other defendants and covenants to satisfy any judgment against the contracting defendant. This case was followed by Rooke J. in Wright (Next Friend of) v. VIA Rail Canada Inc. (2000), 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 166 at 171 (Q.B.). The Court of Appeal reviewed Hart J.'s decision in Amoco Canada Petroleum Co. v. Propak Systems Ltd., 1999 ABQB 716, 1999 CarswellAlta 891, 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 194; affirmed 2001 ABCA 110, 2001 CarswellAlta 575, 281 A.R. 185, 91 Alta. L.R. (3d) 13; leave to appeal refused 2002 CarswellAlta 522, 2002 CarswellAlta 523, 312 A.R. 398 (note) (S.C.C.), and Fruman J.A. gave the following explanation of what she called “proportionate share settlement agreements”, their effect on discovery rights, and the factors to be considered by the courts that review them (at pp. 190-196): Now past is the day when “settlement agreement” can be understood to refer solely to the final resolution of all outstanding issues between all parties to a lawsuit, effectively bringing the suit to an end. In the last several years, in response to increasingly complex and commensurately dilatory and costly litigation, a new generation of settlement agreements has been cautiously adopted by the litigation bar. The new settlement agreements, which include such exotically named species as the Mary Carter agreement and the Pierringer agreement, endeavour to attain a more limited objective: rather than trying to resolve all outstanding issues among all parties, a difficult task in complicated suits, they aim to manage proactively the risk associated with litigation. In short, contracting litigants prefer the certainty of settlement to the uncertainty and expense of a trial and the possibility of an undesirable outcome. This “risk-management” objective is accomplished by settling issues of liability between some but not all of the parties, thereby reducing the number of issues in dispute, simplifying the action, and expediting the suit. Ancillary benefits include a reduction in the financial and opportunity costs associated with complex, protracted litigation, as well as savings of court time and resources. To the extent that a proportionate share settlement agreement completely removes the settling defendants from the suit, it is like a conventional settlement agreement that brings all outstanding issues between the settling parties to a conclusion. Proportionate share settlement agreements therefore typically include the following elements: 1. The plaintiff receives a payment from the settling defendants in full satisfaction of the plaintiff's claim against them; 2. In return, the settling defendants receive from the plaintiff a promise to discontinue proceedings, effectively removing the settling defendants from the suit; 3. Subsequent amendments to the pleadings formally remove the settling defendants from the suit; and 4. The plaintiff then continues its suit against the non-settling defendants. There is, however, an added complication that a proportionate share settlement agreement must address. As a result of third party proceedings, settling defendants are almost always subject to claims for contribution and indemnity from non-settling defendants for the amount of the plaintiff's loss alleged to be attributable to the fault of the settling defendants. Before the settling defendants can be released from the suit, some provision must be made to satisfy these claims. This obstacle is overcome by including an indemnity clause in which the plaintiff covenants to indemnify the settling defendants for any portion of the damages that a court may determine to be attributable to their fault and for which the non-settling defendants would otherwise be liable due to the principle of joint and several liability. Alternatively, the plaintiff may covenant not to pursue the non-settling defendants for that portion of the liability that a court may determine to be attributable to the fault of the settling defendants. It is the latter approach that prevails in the agreement at issue in this suit, but in either case the goal of the proportionate share settlement agreement is to limit the liability of the non-settling party to its several liability. The Competing Positions This court recently considered the validity of a ‘new generation’ settlement agreement in Margetts v. Timmer Estate, [1997] 1 W.W.R. 25, 192 A.R. 42 (Q.B.); affd. (1999), 244 A.R. 114, 209 W.A.C. 114, 178 D.L.R. (4th) 577 (C.A.) There, the trial court recognized and this court affirmed that a tortfeasor has a legitimate and “undoubted right to contract to minimize his financial exposure to the plaintiffs”: at W.W.R. 39. However, in Margetts, supra, the settlement was in the nature of a Mary Carter agreement, which did not completely remove the settling defendants from the suit. As the settling parties continued to be adversarial in interest, a non-settling party remained entitled to full pretrial disclosure from them. In Margetts, therefore, the court did not need to reconcile settlement rights with a non-settling defendant's ability to exercise its pretrial procedural rights in an effort to deflect the plaintiff's accusation of fault. In addition to being grounded in fundamental principles of justice and framed in the Alberta Rules of Court, a non-settling defendant's ability to defend against a suit is anchored in the statutory requirement found in s. 2(1) of the Contributory Negligence Act: 2. (1) When damage or loss has been caused by the fault of 2 or more persons, the court shall determine the degree in which each person was at fault. The effect of this provision is to compel the court to determine the degrees of fault of all contributors to the plaintiffs' damage, whether or not they currently are or ever have been parties to the action. In effect, this provision acts as a safeguard to establish the proportionate share of each defendant's liability, whether settling or non-settling. It therefore becomes apparent that the right to settle, fixing a settling defendant's financial liability to the plaintiff through contract, may have a direct effect on a non-settling defendant's pretrial rights of discovery and production of documents in order to gather evidence to defend the lawsuit. The B.C. Ferry Approach The Canadian cases in which proportionate share settlement agreements have been considered attempt to balance the right to settle against the right to pretrial disclosure. One approach is represented by the decision of the British Columbia Court of Appeal in British Columbia Ferry Corp. v. T & N plc (1995), 65 B.C.A.C. 118, 106 W.A.C. 118, 27 C.C.L.T. (2d) 287 (C.A.). There, the court decided that the non-settling defendants could not maintain a claim for contribution or indemnity against third parties that had settled with the plaintiffs, pursuant to the terms of a proportionate share settlement agreement. However, the court allowed the non-settling defendants to maintain a claim for a declaration to determine the degree to which the plaintiff's damages were attributable to the settling defendants. The court therefore permitted the action for declaratory relief to remain, keeping the settling defendants in the lawsuit for the purely procedural purpose of allowing the non-settling parties access to pretrial procedural rights. The court concluded that the non-settling defendants would be prejudiced in establishing the fault of the third parties, and thus in maintaining their own defence, if they did not retain the benefit of full pretrial procedural rights against the settling parties: at 302. The decision is based on the proposition that it would be “manifestly wrong if a private accord between plaintiff and third party could work to deprive a defendant of the ability to establish an element of proof essential to a just resolution of the action”: at p. 302 (emphasis added). The difficulty with the B.C. Ferry approach is its emphasis on the potential prejudice a non-settling party might suffer. Indeed, it is likely that a non-settling party will always be able to allege some possible disadvantage when it remains as the sole target for liability after other parties abandon the litigation. That is true whether a partial settlement occurs during the course of litigation or even before an action is launched. The B.C. Ferry approach would seem to permit an action for declaratory relief to be maintained for purely procedural purposes against anyone who settled, whether or not they were ever a named party to the litigation, and even though there were no possibility that they might be liable. Litigation, including settlement, is all about advantage, and corresponding disadvantage or prejudice. Settlement, after all, is nothing more than a compromise, in which parties gamble by trading prospective rights for certainty. Nor does prejudice run in only one direction. Failure to allow settlement by parties who want an exit ramp from costly and prolonged litigation may give a party who refuses to settle an even stronger tactical advantage. An unreasonable party can hold the other parties at ransom, virtually dictating the terms of settlement. It is argued that without complete pretrial disclosure a court will be unable to properly apportion the loss. This argument cuts both ways. The plaintiff always bears the burden of proof at trial. By agreeing to remove the settling defendants from the suit and focussing only on the non-settling defendant's alleged misdeeds, a plaintiff runs the risk of no recovery at trial, for it may fail to prove any basis on which a trial court could assign liability to the non-settling party. Decisions to settle with some but not all defendants give rise to challenging issues. What use can be made by the non-settling defendant of settling defendants' discoveries? Will adverse inferences be drawn against the plaintiff if it does not call settling defendants as witnesses? A plaintiff may encounter considerable obstacles in its attempt to recover any damages. It by no means follows that as a result of a partial settlement the non-settling defendant will shoulder a greater portion of the liability than it ought. The B.C. Ferry approach undervalues the importance of settlement. In these days of spiralling litigation costs, increasingly complex cases and scarce judicial resources, settlement is critical to the administration of justice. … Alberta courts have grappled with the B.C. Ferry approach, attempting to balance the certain benefit of settlement against the potential problem of prejudice. Faced with the difficulty of predicting future prejudice, they have looked to the past, assessing such things as the age and complexity of the action; the number of parties involved; how long the present structure of defendants and third parties has been in place; at what stage in the proceedings the application was made; whether discoveries have taken place, documents been produced and expert reports exchanged; whether a trial date has been set; delays and the reason for them; and whether the non-settling party has diligently exercised discovery rights. See Slaferek, supra; Viridian Inc. v. Dresser Canada Inc. (1999), 247 A.R. 23, 73 Alta. L.R. (3d) 348 at p. 363 (Q.B.); Vandevelde v. Smith (1999), 243 A.R. 161 (Q.B.); and Wright, supra. Generally, the longer the action has been in existence and the greater the pretrial disclosure received by the non-settling defendant, the less likely an Alberta judge will find potential prejudice and the more likely the settlement agreement will be given effect…. Indeed, that approach was followed in the present case. The case management judge concluded that because Propak had the advantage of significant oral examination and discovery of documents, it was “clearly better off” than if the settling parties had not been sued or had been formally released by the plaintiffs from the outset, and would not “in any way” be disadvantaged or prejudiced (AB I at 105). This approach has a number of flaws. First, the analysis tends to be superficial and the conclusions unpersuasive. From a pretrial disclosure point of view, most parties will be better off at a more advanced stage in the litigation process. But a non-settling party, although better off, could still be disadvantaged if a court were to truncate its pretrial procedural rights by giving effect to a proportionate share settlement agreement. No matter how dilatory the defendant has been, no matter how interminable its efforts to mine for information, the potential always exists for the next discovery question it asks to be the one that blows the litigation apart. It is difficult for any judge to definitively conclude that there is no potential for prejudice. A second flaw is that this approach always favours settlement at advanced stages rather than earlier stages of litigation. But public policy dictates otherwise. Early settlement means reduced legal costs and less strain on the court system. In modern, complex litigation, it is the pretrial skirmishes that consume most of the court's calendar. … A third flaw is that it gives little guidance to judges, and creates uncertainty for litigants. Because courts are looking at potential rather than actual prejudice, they sometimes have a difficult time evaluating the competing positions. … A test which institutionalizes this degree of uncertainty is no test at all. By properly drafting a proportionate share settlement agreement, settling parties can ensure that a non-settling defendant is responsible only for its proportionate share of the loss. But a non-settling defendant can always assert some form of potential prejudice, which settling parties cannot avoid by contractual means. Litigants will no doubt be reluctant to spend time evaluating their legal position and displaying their hand in settlement negotiations if there is little ability to predict whether a proportionate share settlement agreement will be given effect by the court. The fundamental problem with the current approach is that it requires judges to balance two competing interests, but gives judges few tools with which to do so. The Alberta Rules of Court contain no express rule permitting third party discovery and at least to this point, no one has come up with a creative way of achieving equivalent disclosure by practice note, statute or private agreement. … Alberta's current pretrial disclosure regime severely restricts third party discovery rights. This limitation, which affects all litigants equally, should not be equated to prejudice. Nor should it be used to justify jettisoning proportionate share settlement agreements in this province. A better solution is to introduce some form of third party discovery in Alberta, to address the type of procedural complaints levied in this case. The fact that non-settling defendants are confined to a statutory disclosure regime constrained by the Alberta Rules of Court is not a proper basis for refusing to give effect to proportionate share settlement agreements. It is one thing when the Alberta Rules of Court limit rights of pretrial disclosure. It is another matter entirely when settling parties deliberately thwart a non-settling party's ability to get at the truth. Courts need not countenance agreements containing express provisions that narrow the procedural rights a non-settling defendant would otherwise have or create other obstacles, for example, prohibiting a settling party from cooperating with a non-settling party, participating in interviews, or voluntarily making documents available. A proportionate share settlement agreement should be disclosed to the non-settling party: Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Co. v. Wright, [1997] 10 W.W.R. 622, 120 Man. R. (2d) 214 (Q.B.); affd. (1998), 131 Man. R. (2d) 133, 187 W.A.C. 133 (C.A.). To ensure that the trial judge is aware of the circumstances under which the non-settling defendant has operated, the terms of the agreement, although not necessarily the amount of the settlement, should also be disclosed to the court. Summary In summary, in evaluating proportionate share settlement agreements: 1. A court must keep in mind the strong public policy reason which encourages settlement; 2. The fact that a non-settling defendant has restricted rights of third party disclosure under the Alberta Rules of Court does not justify refusing to give effect to a proportionate share settlement agreement; 3. A court need not approve a proportionate share settlement agreement containing contractual provisions that directly limit the procedural rights a non-settling defendant would otherwise have; and 4. A proportionate share settlement agreement should be disclosed to the non-settling party. To further reduce potential prejudice, the terms of the agreement, although not necessarily the amount of the settlement, should also be disclosed to the court. Her Ladyship then discussed claims for contribution and claims for indemnity, and their relationship to proportionate share settlement agreements. At pp. 196-197, she said: Some confusion exists about claims for contribution and claims for indemnity. Although it is common practice for multiple defendants to issue cross-claims against one another seeking “contribution and indemnity” in respect of the plaintiff's loss, a claim for contribution is usually based on s. 2 of the Contributory Negligence Act and s. 3 of the Tort-feasors Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. T-6. The combined effect of these statutory provisions is the creation of joint and several liability, whereby a plaintiff may claim the whole of its loss from any one defendant, and that defendant may in turn claim contribution from the other defendants in proportion to their respective degree of fault. In contrast to the statutory basis for a claim for contribution, a claim for indemnity is grounded in either contract or tort, arising from an independent duty of care that one defendant or third party owed to another. Proportionate share settlement agreements are relatively straightforward when all defendants are potentially liable to the plaintiff. A settlement is proper so long as the non-settling defendant's liability is strictly limited to the loss it actually caused. The situation is more complicated when the non-settling defendant has issued a third party notice claiming an independent duty that is owed to it, but not to the plaintiff. A settlement cannot extinguish the non-settling defendant's entitlement to indemnification from the third party unless it also extinguishes the non-settling defendant's liability to the plaintiff in respect of claims for which it could seek indemnification from the third party. In Wright (Next Friend of) v. VIA Rail Canada Inc. (2000), 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 166 at 171 (Q.B.), Rooke J. held, at p. 173, that generally “a true Pierringer agreement should result in the amendment of a Statement of Claim and the striking out of a Third Party Notice to exclude the settling defendant.” His Lordship did discuss possible methods of keeping alive the third party proceedings against the settling defendant so as to permit examination for discovery. However, the parties did not wish him to pursue that course of action, so he did not, though His Lordship's comments at pp. 170-71 may be of some interest to future litigants. With respect to the loss of discovery opportunities resulting from the other parties entering into a Pierringer agreement, at p. 177, Rooke J. gave the following warning to litigants: … it seems that the message must go out to such litigants and counsel on their behalf that, if they do not want to take a chance that a co-defendant/third party will settle with the plaintiff and thereby prohibit them from obtaining necessary discovery, they should be diligent in filing Notices to Co-Defendants, Notices to Third Parties, and in obtaining discovery or other procedures of such co-defendant or third parties at the earliest possible opportunity. In Wright (Next Friend of) v. VIA Rail Canada Inc. (2000), 76 Alta. L.R. (3d) 166 at 171 (Q.B.), Rooke J. also addressed the concerns which had been raised by Langston J. in Vandevelde v. Smith (1999), 243 A.R. 161 (Q.B.). At p. 176, His Lordship said: With respect, the answer to these concerns, which appear to relate to real or apprehended inappropriate conduct on the settling parties to take advantage of the non-settling party, is that even in those situations … the Court's discretion remains, as exercised by Langston and Burrows JJ., to dismiss the applications to strike the third party proceedings. In such situations, the result would be that the third party might, for that reason, be required to absorb (at least in the first instance), but for no benefit to itself, the costs involved in remaining a party to the action.
